ev.amr_fc_school.temple.ok: The feast for the priests ate up nearly all the household's stores, but the chief priest took you in his arms himself and promised: "When {g:he|she} is grown, we will take {g:him|her}."
ev.amr_fc_school.ward: Promise you to the {g:"house of youth"|"house of song"}
ev.amr_fc_school.ward.ok: The ward's teachers came, ate tamales, drank hot atole to your health and laughed: "Another {g:warrior|singer} for the ward."
ev.amr_fc_school.title: A promise to the teachers
ev.amr_fc_school.text: Among the Mexica a child is promised to its teachers while still in the cradle. Your parents can hold a feast for the priests and dedicate you to the temple: {g:in the calmecac boys learn writing, the stars and the count of days, but live harshly|at the temple girls weave, sweep the courts and burn copal to the gods}. Or they can promise you to {g:the telpochcalli, your ward's "house of youth", where warriors are raised|your ward's "house of song", where the young learn to sing and dance for the gods}.
ev.amr_fc_school.note: According to Sahagún's Florentine Codex, soon after a birth the Mexica promised the child to the temple school, the calmecac, or to the "house of youth", the telpochcalli, holding a feast for the teachers and priests. Girls too could be dedicated to temple service. Schooling began later, but the promise was considered binding.
ev.amr_fc_school_temple.title: At the temple
ev.amr_fc_school_temple.text: The priests remembered the promise made by your cradle and came for you. {g:In the calmecac you rise before dawn, carry water and branches for the temple fire, learn to paint the signs and count the days|At the temple you rise before dawn, sweep the courts, spin and weave for the gods, and climb the steps with a censer of copal}. It is hard, but you already know things that others do not.
ev.amr_fc_school_ward.title: The ward house
ev.amr_fc_school_ward.text: You have been taken in where you were promised in the cradle. {g:In the "house of youth" you haul firewood and stones for the ward, learn to hold a shield and a wooden sword, and in the evenings you sing and dance at the "house of song"|In the "house of song" the young men and women of the ward gather in the evenings, and you learn the old songs and the dances for the gods}. Now you have a whole band of friends.
ev.amr_fc_thunder.offer: Make an offering on the hill
ev.amr_fc_thunder.offer.ok: On the hilltop they burned a guinea pig, coca leaves and maize and poured chicha over the stones. The thunder grumbled in the distance but came no closer to the village.
ev.amr_fc_thunder.keep: Don't trouble the gods for nothing
ev.amr_fc_thunder.keep.ok: "Thunder rolls where it pleases," the household said. "What a baby needs is a warm cradle." The old people shook their heads and went away.
ev.amr_fc_thunder.title: Child of thunder
ev.amr_fc_thunder.text: You were born in a thunderstorm: lightning struck the slope above the village at the very moment you were first dipped in cold water. The old people say such a child belongs to Illapa, the god of thunder, and may grow up to be his servant or a healer. Illapa must be appeased - an offering burned on the hilltop and chicha poured out - or the thunder will dog the child's steps.
ev.amr_fc_thunder.note: In Andean belief, twins and children born in a thunderstorm belonged to Illapa, god of thunder, lightning and rain; many of them became priests and healers. Spanish "extirpators of idolatry" described this in detail in the early 17th century, but the beliefs themselves are far older. Illapa received offerings of llamas, guinea pigs, coca and maize beer - chicha.
ev.amr_fc_thunder_healer.title: The healer's apprentice
ev.amr_fc_thunder_healer.text: An old healer, himself born in a storm, came for you: "Illapa accepted your family's offering - now he is waiting for you." You are learning from him to tell herbs apart, to read coca leaves, and to divine with a guinea pig what ails a sick person.
ev.amr_fc_thunder_storm.title: Storm on the high pasture
ev.amr_fc_thunder_storm.text: A storm caught you out on the high pasture with the llamas. Lightning struck a rock ten paces away - it knocked you off your feet, but you got up unhurt. Now the village whispers: "Illapa came for what is his," and the old people look at you with wary respect.
